title: Steroids and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Corticosteroids?
excerpt: Can you drink on steroids? How corticosteroids like prednisone, Medrol, and dexamethasone overlap with alcohol, what changes with inhalers, shots, and antibiotics, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on steroids? How prednisone, Medrol, and other corticosteroids interact with alcohol, plus steroid-antibiotic combos and when to get help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the steroids most people are prescribed (corticosteroids such as prednisone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, and hydrocortisone) don't set off a sudden, violent reaction with alcohol. For a healthy adult on a short course, an occasional single drink is unlikely to cause harm, and many doctors are fine with that. The real issue is overlap. Steroids and alcohol both irritate the stomach, raise or swing blood sugar, disturb sleep and mood, weaken the immune system, and thin the bones over time. Add them together and each of those side effects gets bigger. How much that matters depends on three things: which kind of steroid you're on, how long you're taking it, and how much you drink.

**The quick rules:** On a short oral course (a few days to two weeks, including a Medrol dose pack), keep it to an occasional single drink or skip alcohol until you finish. On steroids for weeks, months, or long term, ask your doctor what's safe for you. Inhaled, nasal, skin, and eye steroids barely reach the bloodstream, so normal moderate drinking isn't a concern with them. If you've been given an antibiotic alongside your steroid, check the antibiotic, because some antibiotics are the bigger alcohol problem. And never skip, delay, or stop a steroid dose so you can drink.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance about corticosteroids. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your medicine and knows why you're taking it. **Talk to your doctor before drinking if** you take an oral or injected steroid for more than two weeks, you have diabetes or high blood sugar, you've had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, you also take ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin, or a blood thinner, you have liver disease, or you've been told you have thinning bones. **Get medical help right away if** you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, pass black or tarry stools, have severe stomach pain, are extremely thirsty and urinating far more than usual, have a fever or other signs of a serious infection, notice sudden severe changes in mood or thinking, or you take steroids long term and can't keep your doses down because of vomiting. In an emergency, call 911.

## First, Which "Steroids" Are We Talking About?

The word "steroid" covers two very different families of drugs, and people mix them up all the time.

- **Corticosteroids** are copies of cortisol, the stress hormone your adrenal glands make every day. Doctors prescribe them to calm inflammation and an overactive immune system: for asthma flares, bronchitis, sinus swelling, poison ivy, allergic reactions, back pain, gout, arthritis, eczema, inflammatory bowel disease, and many autoimmune conditions. This is what your pharmacy label means by "steroid," and it's what most of this article is about.
- **Anabolic steroids** are versions of testosterone, used medically for a few specific conditions and used non-medically to build muscle. They work completely differently and carry different risks. There's a short section on them further down.

Within corticosteroids, the way you take the drug matters a lot more than the name:

| Type | Common examples | How much reaches your bloodstream | Alcohol concern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Oral tablets or liquid | Prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone (Medrol), dexamethasone, hydrocortisone | High | Real overlap of side effects; grows with dose and length of course |
| Injections into a vein or muscle | Methylprednisolone, dexamethasone, triamcinolone shots | High for days to weeks | Similar to oral steroids while the dose is active |
| Joint or "cortisone" shots | Triamcinolone, methylprednisolone into a knee, shoulder, or spine | Some, for a few days | Mostly a blood-sugar issue for people with diabetes |
| Inhaled | Fluticasone, budesonide, beclomethasone inhalers | Low | Little to none at usual doses |
| Nasal sprays | Fluticasone (Flonase), mometasone, triamcinolone | Very low | None of note |
| Creams, ointments, eye and ear drops | Hydrocortisone cream, prednisolone eye drops | Very low | None of note |

If you're on an inhaler, nasal spray, or cream, the short version is that alcohol doesn't interact with it in any meaningful way. The rest of this guide is mainly for people taking steroids by mouth or by injection.

## How Steroids and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

Corticosteroids and alcohol don't compete for the same liver enzyme in a way that causes a toxic build-up, and they don't trigger a chemical reaction like the flushing and vomiting you can get from mixing alcohol with metronidazole. Instead, they hit the same body systems from two directions. Here's what that looks like in each one.

### 1. Your stomach lining

Alcohol irritates the stomach lining directly and increases acid. Corticosteroids slow the repair of the stomach lining. On their own, steroids raise the risk of stomach ulcers and bleeding only modestly, but the risk climbs when they're combined with other things that damage the stomach. Alcohol is one of those things. Anti-inflammatory painkillers (ibuprofen, naproxen, aspirin) are another, and they're the bigger one. People on steroids who drink and also take an anti-inflammatory for a hangover headache or a sore joint are stacking three stomach irritants at once. If that's you, read our guide to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) before reaching for the bottle.

### 2. Your blood sugar

Steroids raise blood sugar. They make the liver release more glucose and make your cells respond less to insulin. This is called steroid-induced hyperglycemia, and it's common, especially with higher doses taken in the morning, which push sugar up in the afternoon and evening. Alcohol pushes blood sugar around in the other direction as well: sugary drinks and mixers raise it, while the alcohol itself can stop the liver from releasing glucose and drop it hours later, particularly overnight or if you haven't eaten.

For most people without diabetes, that swing is uncomfortable rather than dangerous. For people with diabetes or prediabetes, it's a real problem. Steroids can push readings very high, and if you're on insulin or a sulfonylurea, drinking can cause a low later on. Readings bouncing in both directions are hard to manage. If you have diabetes and you've been prescribed a steroid, talk to your care team before drinking, and see our [guide to alcohol and blood sugar](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025).

### 3. Your immune system

Steroids work by turning the immune response down. That's the point of taking them, but it also makes it easier to pick up infections and harder to fight them off. Heavy drinking also weakens immune defenses, both in the short term after a binge and over time. If you're on steroids because you're already sick (bronchitis, a sinus infection, a bad asthma flare), drinking heavily asks your body to recover with two handicaps instead of one.

### 4. Sleep and mood

Steroids are well known for causing insomnia, restlessness, irritability, and mood swings, and at higher doses some people feel unusually wired or, less often, low or anxious. Alcohol might make you sleepy at first but breaks up sleep in the second half of the night and can leave you anxious and flat the next day. On a steroid course, that combination often means a short, broken night and a rough, edgy morning. If your sleep is already bad on steroids, our guide on [not being able to sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains why alcohol makes it worse.

### 5. Your bones, over the long run

Long-term corticosteroid use is one of the most common causes of bone thinning that isn't age-related. Heavy drinking over years is also a known risk factor for osteoporosis and fractures, and it raises the chance of falls. This doesn't matter for a one-week course. It matters a lot for people taking steroids for months or years.

### 6. Fluid, blood pressure, and the liver

Steroids can make you hold onto salt and water and can raise blood pressure. Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure too. Steroids are not a well-known cause of liver damage the way acetaminophen is, but both steroids and alcohol can contribute to fat building up in the liver over time, which is one more reason long-term users should keep drinking modest.

## What About Short Courses, Like a Medrol Dose Pack?

This is the most common situation: a few days of prednisone for a flare, or a methylprednisolone (Medrol) dose pack that steps down from six tablets on the first day to one on the last. The courses are short, the doses fall fast, and the long-term risks (bones, adrenal suppression) mostly don't apply.

What does apply:

- **Stomach irritation**, especially if you're also taking an anti-inflammatory painkiller.
- **Blood sugar swings**, especially in the first days when the dose is highest.
- **Sleep and mood**, which are often worst on the high-dose days.
- **The reason you're taking the steroid.** If you're on it for a chest infection, an asthma flare, or a bad allergic reaction, your body is already under strain.

A practical approach for a healthy adult: skip alcohol on the highest-dose days at the start, and if you do drink later in the course, keep it to one drink with food. If you'd rather not think about it, finishing the course first is the simplest option. Most short courses are over within a week or two. We cover the dose pack in more detail in our [methylprednisolone and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/methylprednisolone-and-alcohol), and prednisone specifically in our [prednisone and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/prednisone-and-alcohol).

## Long-Term Steroids and Alcohol

If you take a corticosteroid for months or years (for example for rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, inflammatory bowel disease, polymyalgia, or after a transplant), the picture changes in two ways.

**First, the slow risks add up.** Bone thinning, stomach problems, high blood sugar, weight gain, high blood pressure, and infections all build over time. Regular drinking adds to most of them. Your doctor may already be checking your bones, blood sugar, and blood pressure, and your drinking is useful information for them.

**Second, your body may stop making its own cortisol.** After more than about three weeks of steroid tablets, the adrenal glands can scale back their own output because the medicine is doing the job. That's why you should never stop long-term steroids suddenly, and it's why a bad night of drinking can be riskier for you than for other people. If you vomit repeatedly and can't keep your steroid tablets down, your body may not have enough cortisol to handle the stress. That can tip into a medical emergency called an adrenal crisis, with severe weakness, dizziness, confusion, low blood pressure, and stomach or back pain.

People with adrenal insufficiency, and many people on long-term steroids, are given "sick day rules" for this. If you've been given them, they apply to vomiting after drinking just as they apply to a stomach bug. If you take steroids long term and you're vomiting and can't keep your dose down, seek medical help promptly. Don't wait it out like an ordinary hangover.

## Steroids Plus Antibiotics and Alcohol

Steroids are often prescribed together with an antibiotic, for things like sinus infections, bronchitis, ear infections, or skin infections. If you've been handed both, the antibiotic usually decides the alcohol question, not the steroid.

- **Metronidazole (Flagyl) and tinidazole:** avoid alcohol completely while taking them and for at least three days after your last dose, as their labels advise. Combining them with alcohol can cause flushing, pounding headache, nausea, vomiting, and a racing heart.
- **Linezolid:** avoid tap beer and some wines high in a substance called tyramine, which can cause a dangerous rise in blood pressure with this drug. Ask your pharmacist for the list.
- **Most common antibiotics** (amoxicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, azithromycin, doxycycline, cephalexin) don't cause a dangerous chemical reaction with alcohol. Alcohol can still make side effects like nausea, stomach upset, and dizziness worse, and drinking while you're sick slows recovery.

So with a steroid and an antibiotic together, the safest plan is to hold off on alcohol until both courses are finished, especially as many of these courses are only five to ten days. If you want to know about a specific antibiotic, our [antibiotics and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/antibiotics-and-alcohol) goes drug by drug.

## Cortisone Shots and Alcohol

A cortisone shot into a joint, tendon, or the spine is mostly meant to stay where it's injected, but some of the steroid gets into the bloodstream for a few days. For most people that's not an alcohol issue. A few points are still worth knowing:

- **If you have diabetes,** blood sugar can rise for several days after a joint injection. Alcohol adds to the swings, so check your readings more often that week.
- **The joint needs rest.** Many clinics advise taking it easy for a day or two after the shot. Drinking makes it easier to forget and overdo it.
- **Flushing and a "steroid flare"** (a day or two of extra pain at the injection site) are common side effects. Alcohol doesn't cause them but can make flushing more noticeable.

If your injection was given into a vein or muscle for a systemic problem, such as a bad allergic reaction or an asthma flare, treat it like a course of oral steroids for the next week or so.

## Inhaled, Nasal, and Topical Steroids

These are designed to work where you apply them, and only a small amount reaches the rest of the body. At normal doses, there's no meaningful interaction with moderate drinking.

The more relevant point for inhaler users is that alcohol itself can trigger asthma symptoms in some people, especially with wine and some beers. If you notice wheezing or tightness after drinking, that's worth telling your doctor about. And as always with steroid inhalers, rinse your mouth after using them to prevent thrush. That advice doesn't change on a night out.

## Dexamethasone and Hydrocortisone

Two corticosteroids come up often enough to mention by name.

**Dexamethasone** is a strong, long-acting steroid. It's used for things like severe allergic reactions, croup, brain swelling, some cancers, and to prevent nausea during chemotherapy. A single dose stays active far longer than a dose of prednisone, and the mood and sleep effects can be more pronounced. If you're getting dexamethasone as part of cancer treatment, ask your oncology team about alcohol, because it may also interact with your other medicines and with how you're coping overall.

**Hydrocortisone** tablets are often used as replacement therapy when the adrenal glands don't work properly (adrenal insufficiency or Addison's disease). Here, the steroid replaces a hormone your body needs to survive. Moderate drinking is generally possible, but the sick-day rules above matter even more: vomiting after drinking can mean missed doses, and that can be dangerous.

## Anabolic Steroids and Alcohol

Anabolic steroids aren't the subject of this page, but people search for them under the same words, so here's the honest summary.

Some anabolic steroids taken by mouth are known to stress the liver, and long-term use has been linked to liver damage and, rarely, liver tumors. Heavy drinking stresses the liver too. Anabolic steroids can also raise blood pressure, worsen cholesterol, and affect mood and aggression, and alcohol can push the same things in the wrong direction. If you use anabolic steroids with or without a prescription, the person to ask about alcohol is a doctor who knows exactly what you're taking. Getting your liver enzymes, blood pressure, and cholesterol checked is a sensible step either way.

## How Much Can You Drink on Steroids?

There's no single safe number that applies to everyone, and no official waiting period. Here's a reasonable way to think about it, assuming you're otherwise healthy:

| Situation | General approach |
|---|---|
| Inhaled, nasal, skin, or eye steroid | Normal moderate drinking is generally fine |
| Short oral course or dose pack (under 2 weeks) | Skip high-dose days; otherwise an occasional single drink with food, or wait until you finish |
| Steroid plus antibiotic | Check the antibiotic first; simplest to wait until both are done |
| Oral steroids for weeks to months | Ask your doctor; keep drinking light and infrequent |
| Long-term steroids or adrenal insufficiency | Ask your doctor; know your sick-day rules |
| Diabetes, past ulcer, or also taking NSAIDs or blood thinners | Talk to your doctor before drinking at all |

A few habits help no matter which row you're in:

- **Take your steroid with food,** as most labels advise, and eat if you're drinking.
- **Don't change your dose timing** to fit around a night out. Morning dosing is usually recommended because it fits your body's natural cortisol rhythm and causes less insomnia.
- **Choose your hangover painkiller carefully.** Anti-inflammatories plus steroids plus alcohol is a hard combination for the stomach. Acetaminophen avoids the stomach problem but has its own alcohol limits, which we explain in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).
- **Watch sugary mixers** if your blood sugar is running high on steroids.

## How Long After Steroids Can You Drink?

Once you finish a short course, the drug clears your system quickly. Prednisone and methylprednisolone are mostly gone within a day or so of the last dose, though their effects on the body (like blood sugar and sleep) can take a few days to settle. Dexamethasone lasts longer. A day or two after the last tablet of a short course is a sensible gap for most healthy people.

After a long course, finishing is usually a slow taper rather than a stop, and your adrenal glands may take weeks to months to fully recover. Keep drinking modest during that time and follow your doctor's taper exactly.

## Signs of Trouble: When to Get Help

Most people on steroids who have the occasional drink won't notice anything unusual. These signs are not normal and need attention.

**Get emergency help (call 911) if you have:**

- Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
- Black, tarry, or bloody stools
- Sudden severe stomach pain
- Severe weakness, fainting, confusion, or very low blood pressure while on long-term steroids, especially after vomiting
- Severe confusion, very high blood sugar readings, or signs of a severe infection

**Call your doctor soon if you notice:**

- Ongoing stomach pain, heartburn, or indigestion that's new or worse
- Extreme thirst and urinating much more than usual
- Fever, chills, or an infection that's getting worse rather than better
- Big changes in mood, severe insomnia, or feeling unlike yourself
- Vomiting that means you're missing steroid doses

These can look like a bad hangover at first. If you're on steroids and something feels more serious than a normal rough morning, don't brush it off.

## Can DHM Help When You're on Steroids?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data. It's promising, not proven, and there's no good evidence that it reduces any of the specific risks of combining alcohol with corticosteroids, such as stomach bleeding, blood sugar swings, or lowered immunity.

There also isn't much research on how DHM interacts with prescription drugs in people. If you're on steroids for a serious or long-term condition, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) explains what's known and what isn't.

If you're between courses, or on a low-risk steroid like an inhaler, and you want to try DHM for occasional nights out, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take. No supplement changes the advice above: drink less, eat, and follow your steroid prescription exactly.

## The Bottom Line

- Corticosteroids and alcohol don't cause a sudden dangerous reaction, but they share side effects: stomach irritation, blood sugar swings, poor sleep, mood changes, lower immunity, and, over time, bone thinning.
- Inhaled, nasal, skin, and eye steroids don't meaningfully interact with moderate drinking.
- On a short course or dose pack, skip the high-dose days and keep it to an occasional single drink with food, or wait until you finish.
- If you're also on an antibiotic, check it. Metronidazole and tinidazole mean no alcohol at all.
- On long-term steroids, ask your doctor, keep drinking light, and know what to do if you vomit and can't keep your dose down.
- Be extra careful with diabetes, a history of ulcers, or anti-inflammatory painkillers.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking steroids?**

For most healthy adults on a short course of a corticosteroid like prednisone or methylprednisolone, an occasional single drink with food is unlikely to cause harm. The concern is that steroids and alcohol share side effects, including stomach irritation, blood sugar swings, poor sleep, and lowered immunity, so drinking makes those worse. If you take steroids for more than two weeks, have diabetes, have had a stomach ulcer, or take anti-inflammatory painkillers, talk to your doctor before drinking.

**Can I drink alcohol with steroids and antibiotics together?**

Check the antibiotic first, because it usually matters more than the steroid. Metronidazole and tinidazole should not be combined with alcohol at all, during the course and for at least three days afterward. Most other common antibiotics, such as amoxicillin, azithromycin, and doxycycline, don't cause a dangerous reaction, but alcohol can worsen side effects and slow your recovery. The simplest plan is to wait until both courses are finished.

**Can I drink on a Medrol dose pack?**

A methylprednisolone dose pack lasts six days and starts at its highest dose, so it's best to skip alcohol on the first few days. Later in the pack, one drink with food is unlikely to cause problems for a healthy adult. If you're on it for an infection, asthma flare, or allergic reaction, or you also take ibuprofen or naproxen, it's simpler to wait until the pack is finished.

**Is it safe to drink after a cortisone shot?**

For most people, yes, in moderation. A joint or spine injection mostly stays where it's injected, though a little reaches the bloodstream for a few days. People with diabetes should watch their blood sugar closely that week, since both the shot and alcohol can push readings around. Rest the joint as advised, and treat a steroid injection into a muscle or vein for a systemic problem like a short course of oral steroids.

**Can you drink alcohol with a steroid inhaler or nasal spray?**

Yes. Inhaled and nasal steroids like fluticasone and budesonide act mainly where they're applied, and very little reaches the bloodstream, so they don't meaningfully interact with moderate drinking. Be aware that alcohol itself can trigger asthma symptoms in some people, and keep rinsing your mouth after using a steroid inhaler.

**How long after finishing steroids can I drink alcohol?**

After a short course, prednisone and methylprednisolone clear the body within about a day, though effects on sleep and blood sugar can take a few days to settle. Waiting a day or two after the last dose is a sensible gap for most healthy people. After a long course, you'll usually taper off slowly, and your body may take weeks or longer to fully recover its own cortisol production, so keep drinking modest and follow your doctor's plan.

**Does alcohol make steroids less effective?**

Alcohol doesn't block corticosteroids from working in a direct chemical way. But heavy drinking can undermine what the steroid is treating, for example by worsening inflammation in the gut, irritating the airways in some people with asthma, or weakening your ability to fight an infection. It can also make side effects worse, which can make the course harder to finish.

**What about anabolic steroids and alcohol?**

Anabolic steroids are a different family of drugs from the corticosteroids most people are prescribed. Some oral anabolic steroids can stress the liver, and they can raise blood pressure and affect cholesterol and mood. Heavy drinking pushes many of the same things in the wrong direction. If you use anabolic steroids, talk to a doctor who knows exactly what you take and get your liver, blood pressure, and cholesterol checked.
